meta.title: Conflict Watchlist
meta.notes: Fully automated register: a scheduled open-source review rewrites this file daily (procedure in docs/WATCHLIST-REVIEW.md) and an hourly GitHub Action refreshes the live reporting feed (watchlist-live.json) from GDELT. Every comparison the dashboard shows (state moves, changed dimensions, the attention-score bonuses) is made against the register as it stood compareDays (7) days ago, taken from each item's `snapshots` (one entry per review: date, state and the five dimensions). Each review: (1) set reviewDate/previousReviewDate, (2) for every item set the new `now` on the five dimensions and the new `state`, then append today's snapshot (keep the last 60), (3) rewrite `status` (`summary`: plain-language current status whose first sentence states the newest development; `sources`: 2–3 links to the newest reporting), `whyNow`, `topic` and `whyMatters` (stable framing, revise only on a phase change), `changes` (dated bullets covering the last 7 days: keep those still inside the window, add today's, drop older ones), `next`, `ignore` and `sources`, (4) record any state move in `history` and keep `timeline` (4–8 dated one-line events of the current phase, chronological) current. The dashboard derives attention rank, movements, changed-dimension flags, staleness, coverage surges — do not type those in. `next` holds named, checkable indicators.

Priority.desc: Direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value.

Active.desc: Material trend, escalation, or regional relevance.

Watch.desc: Baseline monitoring; no current learning priority.

Archive.desc: Reserve — retained for reference and pattern work; revisit only on a named trigger.

phase.label: Conflict phase
phase.desc: A short label for the stage the conflict is in (for example attritional war, ceasefire without implementation, grey-zone contest). It sits under the current-status summary and shows the label from 7 days ago when it changed.

escalation.label: Escalation risk
escalation.desc: How likely a step up in intensity or a change of phase is in the coming weeks.

levels.Low: Stable; no live trigger and restraints hold.
levels.Moderate: Triggers exist (deadlines, disputes, incidents) but restraints are holding.
levels.High: Active exchanges or a named trigger that is likely to fire; a phase change is plausible within weeks.
levels.Severe: Active war or ongoing kinetic exchange with strategic stakes (major shipping lanes, energy, great-power forces).

tempo.label: Operational tempo
tempo.desc: How much military activity is actually happening in the review window.

levels.Medium: Recurring incidents or steady, limited operations (patrols, fortification, occasional strikes).
levels.High: Daily strikes or operations across fronts.

adaptation.label: Adaptation behaviour
adaptation.desc: How much new tactical or technical behaviour appeared in the window; this is where the Army learning sits.

levels.Low: Both sides are using the same methods as before.
levels.High: Novel, repeatable adaptations appeared (new weapons employment, counter-measures, doctrine shifts).

sgExposure.label: Singapore exposure
sgExposure.desc: How directly the conflict touches Singapore's interests. Not shown as a register column; it still feeds the attention score and the expanded row.

levels.Moderate: An ASEAN or diplomatic role, observer contributions, or supply-chain spillover.
levels.High: Direct effect on sea lanes, energy or shipping, a Singapore-flagged vessel affected, or relevance to deployments.

attentionScore.desc: Deterministic, explainable rank. state (Priority 40 / Active 25 / Watch 10 / Archive 0) + escalation risk (Severe 20 / High 15 / Moderate 8 / Low 2) + 5 per dimension that changed over the last 7 days (compareDays) + 10 if the state moved up over the same window + Singapore exposure (High 8 / Moderate 4 / Low 0) + tier (T1 6 / T2 3 / T3 0) + 8 if the live open-source feed shows a coverage surge (see definitions.feed.surgeRule). Items flagged ignore-for-now are shown but ranked last.

feed.source: GDELT DOC 2.0 API (open, no key). Per item: 30-day daily article counts (TimelineVolRaw) and the most relevant English-language articles of the last 7 days (ArtList, HybridRel). Synced by .github/workflows/sync-watchlist-feed.yml into watchlist-live.json.
feed.surgeRule: A coverage surge is flagged when the last 7 days carry at least twice the article volume of the 7 days before and at least 20 articles; a surge adds 8 points to the attention score.
feed.titleFilter: Articles are kept only when the title contains one of the item's terms, to cut GDELT's full-text noise.
feed.terms: Title filter: at least one of these substrings must appear in an article title for it to count as reporting on the item.
feed.require: Optional groups of substrings; a title must contain at least one term from every group (two-party theatres: one term per side).
feed.exclude: Optional substrings that drop a title (sport, entertainment and other noise), in addition to the sync's global list.
feed.spamDomainsNote: Article sources dropped outright (livestream/score spam). The daily review adds domains seen producing noise.

columns.tier: Standing relevance to the Army: T1 Priority Conflicts, T2 Active Regional & Escalation Watches, T3 Baseline Regional Research Reserve. Tiers do not change week to week.
columns.state: Today's monitoring state: Priority (direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value), Active (material trend, escalation or regional relevance), Watch (baseline monitoring), Archive (reserve; revisit on a named trigger). ▲▼ marks a move over the last 7 days.
columns.status: Current status: the newest title-matched headline from the live open-source feed (synced hourly) on top, then a plain-language summary of what is happening now whose first sentence states the newest development, with links to the newest reporting it rests on. The phase label sits beneath; a struck-through label is the phase 7 days ago.
columns.coverage: Open-source coverage from the live feed (GDELT with Google News fallback): the sparkline is the last 30 days (or four weekly counts), the number is articles in the last 7 days with the change against the 7 before. 'Surge' = at least twice the prior week and at least 20 articles. Refreshes hourly.
columns.nextIndicator: The soonest dated indicator to watch, tagged with the numbered topic and watch area it informs (or 'cross-cutting' when it bears on the theatre as a whole). Expand the row for the full list.
columns.confidence: How well-sourced the assessment is: High (multiple independent, dated sources), Medium (some single-source or snippet-only items), Low (thin or contested reporting).
columns.attention: Attention score, the register's sort order. Hover a score for its breakdown.
columns.topic: Topics of interest: the three capability contests the Army follows this theatre for, set by the team (from the watchlist workbook). Numbered so they line up with the 'Why it matters' and 'Watch areas' columns; the chip is the topic's adaptability rating.
columns.whyMatters: Why it matters here: for each numbered topic, what the theatre tests (the capability, behaviour or mechanism under study).
columns.watchAreas: Watch areas: for each numbered topic, its watch status and what to monitor. Status tags: Rising (activity increasing), Established (steady pattern), Contested (the outcome is still open), Watch for trigger (review only on a named event), Background monitor, Declining.
columns.adaptability: Adaptability: how transferable the topic's lessons are to the Army — High, Medium or Low, set by the team.

infoOps.desc: Information operations and strategic communications watch. Switched on for an item when a trigger event (a summit, a crisis) makes messaging and influence activity worth tracking on its own: a narrower hourly feed of reporting on official messaging, state-media narratives and documented influence campaigns, plus dated findings and an assessment researched daily from open sources.

types.official statement: Government, foreign-ministry, military or party statement aimed at an audience (strategic communications).
types.state-media narrative: Framing pushed by state or party media, including English-language outlets aimed abroad.
types.covert information operation: Documented coordinated inauthentic behaviour, disinformation or cognitive-warfare activity, attributed by a credible reporter.
types.coercive signalling: Military, coast-guard or legal action whose purpose is the message it sends.
types.sanctions/lawfare: Sanctions, lists or legal framing used to pressure or delegitimise.
types.counter-messaging: The targeted side's official response or rebuttal.
types.domestic narrative: Narratives inside the targeted polity (parties, polls, viral claims).
types.debunked claim: A specific false claim identified by a fact-checker.
types.third-party assessment: Analysis by a think-tank, researcher or major outlet.

items.whyNow: Russia's strike campaign has switched its main effort to Kyiv's communications: on 27 Sep, the fourth consecutive night of attacks on the capital, Zelensky counted 277 drones in 24 hours, 155 of them jet-powered, a Kyiv data centre was hit twice, Kyivstar's headquarters was struck and Russia's defence ministry confirmed hitting a Vodafone Ukraine data centre, while ISW read the pattern as Putin pivoting to a long-range-strike theory of victory for winter 2026–27 as Ukraine claimed 10,660 Russian casualties in a week and 125 sq km recovered under Operation Vivaldi, and Lavrov brushed off the first Russian–German foreign-minister meeting since 2022.
changes: 27 Sep: Russian drones and missiles hit Kyiv for a fourth consecutive night; a strike on the Stolichny market killed two and injured four, nine were injured across the capital, a data centre was struck twice in the morning wounding two children and an adult, Kyivstar said its headquarters was hit without casualties and Russia's defence ministry confirmed striking a Vodafone Ukraine data centre, with outages affecting about 100,000 households; Zelensky said Russia launched 277 drones since 26 Sep, 155 of them jet-powered, hitting two kindergartens, two schools, communications facilities and the Saudi ambassador's residence, and that October sanctions will target Russia's ballistic-missile supply chain (Kyiv Independent, Ukrinform, Reuters via Moscow Times).

27 Sep: AP counted at least six killed overnight and on Sunday: one in Kyiv, one in Vyshneve, one in Odesa region, a woman and a 16-year-old girl killed by guided bombs in Sumy and a woman killed by a Ukrainian drone in Enerhodar; Lavrov dismissed his meeting with German foreign minister Wadephul in New York, thought to be the first since 2022 and held at Berlin's request, saying Wadephul 'simply reiterated his official position condemning Russia' (AP via ABC News); Zelensky said Russia fired over 2,200 drones, about 1,650 guided bombs and 38 missiles in the week and faulted China, India, Brazil and South Africa for lacking 'a consistently strong position' (Kyiv Post).

27 Sep: Zelensky said Ukrainian forces killed or wounded 10,660 Russian troops in the week, citing Drapatyi, and that Operation Vivaldi has recovered 125 sq km north of Lyman with 50 sq km formally de-occupied, Shandryholove, Derylove and Serednie retaken and Drobysheve fully controlled at a cost to Russia of over 3,000 troops, Biletsky calling it 'the first' of four seasons; the General Staff reported 221 engagements, 26 each in the Kostiantynivka and Pokrovsk sectors, and strikes on 26–27 Sep on a drone storage-and-launch facility in Donetsk city, ammunition depots at Krepensk and Luhansk, a logistics depot at Rovenky, a fuel depot at Novoamvrosiivsk and a P-18 radar (Kyiv Post, Kyiv Independent, Ukrinform).

26 Sep: Russia launched 173 drones, about 50 jet-powered, killing two women in Zaporizhzhia and two people in Sumy, while ArcelorMittal halted its Kryvyi Rih works after four missile strikes in five weeks; Ukraine's General Staff reported hits on the Azov optical-mechanical plant of the Tactical Missiles Corporation and the Ilsky refinery, which halted; Zelensky said Russia will spend $12bn on jet drones and loitering munitions in 2027 against a 55% Ukrainian interception rate for jet-powered Shaheds (single source) and that Putin 'always has some pretext' not to hold a three-way meeting; Trump declined to confirm the Patriot licence (Al Jazeera, Kyiv Independent, CNN); ISW assessed that Ukraine's 2026 gains may be forcing Putin to rely on a winter long-range-strike campaign that depends on jet-powered Gerans penetrating at scale, and that Ukrainian forces now target Russian reinforcement of infiltrations rather than clearing them at once; US and Ukrainian officials denied a Bloomberg report that Trump asked Zelensky to travel to Moscow (ISW via Kyiv Post).

25 Sep: Russian drones killed seven in Kyiv, including a 14-year-old (Ukrinform, Kyiv Independent); Zelensky and Peskov both confirmed a US proposal for technical-level trilateral talks, possibly in the UAE, without a date (Al Jazeera, Ukrainska Pravda); Putin said Ukraine 'should be made to feel Russia's retaliatory strikes' and that Russia is 'not preparing for any kind of hostilities with Europe' (Meduza); the General Staff confirmed hits on the Lukoil Perm and Novoshakhtinsk refineries (Ukrinform); Zelensky said Trump had made a 'final decision' on Patriot production licences (Kyiv Post).

24 Sep: Russia's attack with 282 drones, four Zircons and three ballistic missiles killed 16 and injured 59 across Ukraine; Peskov said Moscow seeks 'peace, not a temporary ceasefire' after Lavrov ruled out any pause during talks; ISW called Russian claims of encircling Dobropillia cognitive warfare; suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova (Kyiv Independent, ISW via Kyiv Post).

next.text: Date and venue of the US-proposed technical-level trilateral round confirmed by Kyiv and the Kremlin on 25 Sep (UAE mooted) after Zelensky's 26 Sep 'pretext' charge and the 26 Sep denial that Trump asked him to go to Moscow; whether an energy and telecoms strike moratorium is on the agenda after Lavrov's 27 Sep dismissal of the Wadephul meeting.
next.ifSeen: Round convened with a moratorium on the agenda → phase check and flag this week; no date by end-October → expect the winter strike campaign ISW described on 26 Sep to open unchecked.

next.text: The telecoms campaign of 23–27 Sep (Datagroup, Cosmonova, Kyivstar headquarters, Vodafone Ukraine data centre) produces a nationwide mobile or internet outage lasting over 24 hours, or extends to heating plants and gas production as the ISW-described winter long-range-strike theory of victory takes shape, or Russia repeats a 250+ drone day on Kyiv with a ballistic wave twice in one week.
next.ifSeen: Escalate; data-centre and core-network failover, the 100,000-household outage figure of 27 Sep and the ballistic interception rate over Kyiv become the metrics for layered defence and dispersed support.

next.text: Jet-powered drones were 155 of 277 (56%) on 26–27 Sep and 76 of 162 on 25 Sep; whether Ukraine's interception rate against them (55% on 26 Sep per Zelensky, 44 of 76 on 25 Sep per the Air Force) rises above 75% through scaled jet-drone interceptors, or stays flat while the jet share holds above half of raids for a month.
next.ifSeen: Rate rises → note for the monthly pattern set on interceptor drones as the primary counter; jet share holds above half with the rate flat → escalate on the 2027 $12bn Russian programme.

next.text: The Patriot production licence Zelensky announced on 25 Sep, which Trump declined to confirm on 26 Sep, put in writing (DSCA notification or a Raytheon/Ukrainian partner announcement), and the October sanctions package on Russia's ballistic-missile supply chain Zelensky flagged on 27 Sep adopted by the EU or US.
next.ifSeen: Licence confirmed → note for the monthly pattern set on sovereign interceptor production; left unconfirmed by Washington → track only.

next.text: CEC final Duma results (due by 5 Oct) followed by a Russian mobilisation decree or covert call-up of the 300,000 Macron called 'plausible' on 24 Sep, given Zelensky's 27 Sep claim of 10,660 Russian casualties in a week and over 300,000 in 2026, or Ukraine's own mobilisation changes enacted.
next.ifSeen: Decree → escalate and phase check; no decree but regional call-up orders → monthly pattern note on force generation under attrition.

next.text: Vivaldi's 'second season' after Biletsky's 27 Sep remark: a 3rd Army Corps push toward the Zherebets line or east of Sloviansk, or a Russian shift south toward Sloviansk; a verified Russian advance toward Dobropillia beyond the local gain ISW recorded southeast of the town on 25 Sep; ISW confirmation that the Ukrainian tactic of striking Russian reinforcement of infiltrations, noted on 26 Sep, is repeated in a second sector.
next.ifSeen: Phase check: attritional stalemate versus an operational-level shift; tactic repeated → note for the monthly pattern set on counter-infiltration.

next.text: Further NATO airspace or hybrid incidents after the Mi-8 over Poland (23 Sep), drone crashes in Romania and Moldova (24 Sep) and the Leipzig airport drone attempt Berlin blamed on the Kremlin, following Lavrov's 27 Sep dismissal of German de-escalation calls: a NATO shoot-down over Poland, an Article 4 consultation, or a hybrid strike on a supporter state.
next.ifSeen: Alliance-response dimension → escalate if a shoot-down or consultation occurs.

timeline.text: Russia hit Kyiv with 32 cruise missiles and 166 Shahed-type drones, over half jet-powered, killing five and ending the three-day pause declared during US envoys Witkoff and Kushner's visits to Moscow and Kyiv.
Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps revealed Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive near Lyman it said cleared 75 square kilometres of Russian infiltrators and liberated Serednie and nearby villages.

A Ukrainian drone strike set both crude distillation units ablaze at Gazprom Neft's Moscow refinery, followed on 22 September by strikes on the Ufa and Samara refineries more than 900 kilometres from the border.

Zelensky met Trump at the UN General Assembly and offered a reciprocal energy ceasefire, which Lavrov answered the next day by saying Russia would not pause its operation during negotiations in any format.
Russia launched 282 drones and three waves of ballistic and Zircon missiles, killing 16 people across Ukraine including two in Kyiv, while suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova.

Russian drones killed seven people in Kyiv as Ukraine's General Staff confirmed strikes on the Lukoil Perm refinery 1,450 kilometres from the border, and Kyiv and the Kremlin both confirmed a US proposal for technical-level trilateral talks.

Russia launched 173 drones, about 50 of them jet-powered, killing four people, while Ukraine's General Staff reported hits on the Azov optical-mechanical plant and the Ilsky refinery and Zelensky said Russia will spend $12bn on jet drones in 2027.

On the fourth consecutive night of strikes on Kyiv Russia launched 277 drones in 24 hours, 155 of them jet-powered, hit a Kyiv data centre twice and Kyivstar's headquarters, and Lavrov dismissed German de-escalation calls, while Zelensky said Operation Vivaldi had recovered 125 square kilometres north of Lyman.

text: On persistent ISR versus signature management and deception, the Established and Contested status holds and the contest is moving to counter-infiltration. ISW on 26 Sep found Ukrainian forces now striking Russian attempts to reinforce initial infiltrations rather than clearing infiltrators at once, with Russian milbloggers blaming false reporting for losses north of Lyman, where Zelensky on 27 Sep claimed 125 sq km recovered and 10,660 Russian casualties in a week (unverified). Persistent observation is punishing reinforcement more than concealment protects it. On EW versus alternative UAS control and layered counter-UAS, the Rising rating is confirmed by the jet-drone share crossing half: 155 of 277 drones on 26–27 Sep and 76 of 162 on 25 Sep were jet-powered, against interception rates of 55% on 26 Sep (single source) and 44 of 76 on 25 Sep, which ISW judged the basis of Russia’s winter theory of victory.

On contested sustainment versus dispersed support and repair, targeting has shifted from energy to communications: a Kyiv data centre was hit twice on 27 Sep, Kyivstar’s headquarters was struck and Russia confirmed hitting a Vodafone Ukraine data centre, after Datagroup and Cosmonova on 23–26 Sep, with about 100,000 households cut off. Ukraine answered on 26–27 Sep with a drone launch site in Donetsk city, four depots and a P-18 radar. Dispersed civil networks are absorbing the hits; throughput under a winter campaign is untested.

items.whyNow: Targeted killing and a fight over who runs Gaza, not implementation, set the tempo two weeks before the truce's first anniversary: on 27 Sep the IDF and Shin Bet confirmed that a 26 Sep Nuseirat strike killed Saher Nidal Saqr, filmed carrying Noa Argamani into Gaza on 7 Oct 2023, and that Hamas commander Muhammad Ghabain, who held nine hostages, died in a northern Gaza strike on 22 Sep, two more Palestinians were killed as Gaza's health ministry passed 74,016 dead, Smotrich called for Israel to 'go to war' in the West Bank and 'do there what we did in Gaza' with annexation up to the Yellow Line, which Egypt rejected the same day, and UNRWA's acting chief pushed back on the Board of Peace's exclusion.
changes: 27 Sep: The IDF and Shin Bet said a 26 Sep strike in Nuseirat, with the police Gideonim unit, killed Saher Nidal Saqr, filmed riding the motorcycle that carried Noa Argamani and Avinatan Or into Gaza on 7 Oct 2023, describing him as affiliated with 'global jihadist' groups, a weapons supplier to Hamas and 'recently' planning attacks in violation of the ceasefire, and that strikes in northern Gaza on 22 Sep killed Hamas military-wing commander Muhammad Hamad Muhammad Ghabain, who had held nine named hostages including the Berman twins, Agam Berger and Alon Ohel; the IDF also released drone footage it said shows a child carrying weapons into a home in central Gaza (Times of Israel, ynet); Palestinian media had reported Saqr's death on 26 Sep before any Israeli confirmation (ynet).

27 Sep: Israeli strikes killed two Palestinians and wounded seven: a drone hit a vehicle on al-Aqsa Street in the Tel al-Hawa industrial area of Gaza City, killing Uday Adli al-Assar, 28, and a strike in al-Mawasi west of Khan Younis killed one and wounded three, with the IDF saying both targeted Hamas operatives; drones also wounded five near tents at the Sheikh Radwan market and two at the White Mosque in al-Shati (Anadolu, Middle East Monitor, Middle East Eye, AP via ABC News); Gaza's health ministry said on 26 Sep the toll had reached 74,016 killed and 175,068 wounded, and AP cited 1,145 killed since the 10 Oct 2025 truce, a figure that conflicts with WAFA's 1,394 on 26 Sep and Al Jazeera's 'nearly 1,451' on 27 Sep; Netanyahu repeated that forces 'will not withdraw until Hamas disarms' (AP via ABC News, Al Jazeera).

27 Sep: Finance Minister Smotrich told ynet Israel must 'go to war in Judea and Samaria, to do there what we did in Gaza', dismantle the Palestinian Authority as 'a terror authority' and annex territory up to the Yellow Line in Gaza and the Litani in Lebanon; Egypt's foreign ministry the same day rejected Israeli calls to expand West Bank operations and undermine the PA, the Palestinian foreign ministry called the remarks 'dangerous calls for war', and Crisis Group's Zonszein and Chatham House's Mekelberg cautioned against reading them as mere pre-election posturing (Al Jazeera, The National, Daily News Egypt); UNRWA acting chief Christian Saunders said the agency's capabilities are 'difficult to replicate' after the Board of Peace's 25 Sep exclusion, a Board official told AP its members had nonetheless met UNRWA several times, and the Jerusalem Post reported the Atalef drone that killed two reservists on 24 Sep had at least seven prior non-detonations and three explosions during examination in 2025 (Al Jazeera, AP via ABC News, Jerusalem Post).

26 Sep: The IDF said a strike on Nuseirat killed Ibrahim Fawzi Ismail Mohsen, a Nukhba Force member, and a strike in Khan Younis killed Hamas operative Mohammed Kamel Suleiman Mohsen, both accused of restoring Hamas infrastructure (Times of Israel); Anadolu reported Mohsen was killed by a drone at Al-Sawarha cemetery; an evening drone strike west of Nuseirat killed a Palestinian, WAFA putting the toll at 73,914 (Anadolu, WAFA); Hamas spokesman Hazem Qassem condemned the Board of Peace's refusal to work with UNRWA as 'complete alignment with the Zionist position' and Khalil al-Hayya said the roadmap, 'the issue of weapons' included, must be implemented 'as a package' through statehood (Al Jazeera, Times of Israel, single source).

25 Sep: An Israeli strike on a vehicle at the Wijdan displacement camp in al-Mawasi killed one Palestinian (Arab News, WAFA); the IDF said two reservists were killed on 24 Sep when their Atalef FPV drone crashed on take-off in the northern buffer zone and exploded when picked up, grounded all small explosive drones for 48 hours pending a brigadier-general-led inquiry (Times of Israel, JNS); the IDF and Shin Bet said they have killed 16 'key' Hamas financial officers who moved over $1bn (Times of Israel); the New York Times corroborated Haaretz's report that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed warned Netanyahu of a 'major attack' about a week before 7 Oct 2023, which Netanyahu's office denies (Haaretz, Times of Israel).

24 Sep: Netanyahu told UNGA that genocide allegations are 'the biggest lie of the century'; Hamas said it is 'fully ready' to implement the roadmap and demanded entry of the technocratic committee and the international force (CBS, Jerusalem Post); Blair told a Board of Peace event that Hamas 'has agreed' to the destruction of its tunnels and weapons factories, Mladenov said the Board works to no timetable, and ISF commander Jeffers said 500 troops from Morocco and Kosovo have completed training (ynet, Yeshiva World, Jerusalem Post); on 23 Sep the Board unveiled a $2.4bn, 66-project reconstruction plan conditioned on Hamas disarmament and an Israeli strike killed Hamas finance chief Mohammad Abu Elwan (Al Jazeera).

next.text: First anniversary of the ceasefire — Board of Peace progress assessment after Mladenov's 24 Sep 'no timetable' line, Blair's 24 Sep claim that Hamas agreed to tunnel destruction, al-Hayya's 26 Sep 'package' formula and Netanyahu's 27 Sep 'no withdrawal until Hamas disarms'.
next.ifSeen: Assessment names Israeli non-implementation → phase stays 'without implementation'; flag this week if the Board suspends the roadmap or Hamas formally rejects the disarmament sequence.

next.text: ISF advance elements (500 trained Moroccan and Kosovar troops per Jeffers on 24 Sep) enter the Rafah pilot zone under the sector-by-sector demilitarisation plan, or the Board confirms slippage to after the Israeli election as its officials conceded in September.
next.ifSeen: First third-party force in Gaza → monthly pattern note on stabilisation-force entry; slippage past October → Board of Peace credibility falls.

next.text: IDF expert-team inquiry into the 24 Sep Atalef FPV explosion reports: attribution to Hamas electronic interference versus the fuzing failures the Jerusalem Post documented on 27 Sep (seven non-detonations, three explosions on examination in 2025), and whether the 48-hour grounding of small explosive drones is lifted with new handling or counter-EW procedures.
next.ifSeen: EW attribution → note for the monthly pattern set on adversary counter-UAS in a truce; fuzing or handling failure → note on FPV safety at scale, track only.

timeline.text: The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, endorsing the US Gaza plan, welcoming the Board of Peace and authorising an International Stabilization Force for Gaza.
Israel's security cabinet approved entry of an initial International Stabilization Force of about 200 personnel from countries such as Uganda and Morocco, operating in coordination with the IDF.
Hamas approved the Board of Peace's plan pairing gradual disarmament with phased Israeli withdrawal, a plan Netanyahu rejected pending genuine disarmament.
UN humanitarian officials said Israel had pushed the yellow line inward, leaving Palestinians under 40 percent of Gaza, with 1,334 killed since the ceasefire.

The Board of Peace unveiled a $2.4bn, 66-project reconstruction plan conditioned on Hamas disarmament, while an Israeli strike in western Khan Younis killed senior Hamas finance official Mohammad Abu Elwan among seven dead that day.

Netanyahu told the UN General Assembly that genocide allegations are the biggest lie of the century, while Tony Blair told a Board of Peace event that Hamas had agreed to the destruction of its tunnels and weapons factories and Hamas demanded entry of the technocratic committee and the international force.

The IDF said it had killed 16 key Hamas financial officers and grounded all small explosive drones after two reservists were killed by their own FPV drone, and the next day strikes in Nuseirat and Khan Younis killed two Hamas operatives as Hamas condemned the Board of Peace for excluding UNRWA.

The IDF and Shin Bet confirmed that a Nuseirat strike had killed a man filmed abducting Noa Argamani on 7 October 2023 and that a Hamas commander who held nine hostages had died in northern Gaza, as two more Palestinians were killed, the toll passed 74,000 and Smotrich called for a Gaza-style war in the West Bank.

timeline.text: The US and Iran signed a 14-point memorandum of understanding that lifted the US naval blockade, reopened the Strait of Hormuz and opened a 60-day negotiating period.
After Iranian strikes on vessels collapsed the June ceasefire, US Central Command resumed its naval blockade of Iranian ports and struck Iranian anti-shipping targets near Hormuz.
US strikes on Iranian coastal radars killed 11 people, including five at a wedding in Kuhestak; the IRGC answered with missile and drone attacks on US bases in Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq and Kuwait.
After the IRGC fired anti-ship ballistic missiles at a US carrier and destroyer, CENTCOM destroyed or disabled three Iranian tankers, the Downy, Stark 1 and Kylo.

A day after Witkoff and Kushner held Qatari-mediated talks with Araghchi in New York, Iran handed the US a written road map for a regionwide ceasefire and phased Hormuz reopening, while the bulk carrier Cape Dao was hit off Musandam and one seafarer was killed.

Foreign Minister Araghchi put a 'concrete' seven-day plan to Washington to end hostilities, lift the blockade and reopen Hormuz before nuclear talks, a senior official ruled out any nuclear concessions, and Iraq's four airports cut all Iranian flights under US sanctions.

Trump publicly rejected Iran's seven-day plan, saying Tehran wants the strait opened immediately because it is 'losing so badly', after the Wall Street Journal reported he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms.

The IRGC claimed to have captured a second US underwater drone in the strait, which CENTCOM called 'clearly desperate', while Trump said talks would resume this week and Iran's UN delegation said no new round was planned.

text: On long-range strike versus integrated air and missile defence, the Established · Contested status is borne out by rhetoric rather than fire: no strike on Iranian soil or IRGC launch at a Gulf host was reported through 27 Sep, yet army spokesman Akraminia's promise on 27 Sep of a 'more crushing, extensive and decisive response' and the Wall Street Journal's 26 Sep report that munitions depth is shaping a post-midterm strike decision show both sides sizing the next exchange against magazines. On maritime chokepoint disruption versus energy-route resilience, the status holds and the contest has moved under water: the IRGC's 27 Sep claim of a second captured autonomous vehicle, denied by CENTCOM as 'clearly desperate', points to a sensing and mine-countermeasure layer beneath the convoys, while Energy Secretary Wright's figure of nearly 13 million b/d (single source) sits beside Al Arabiya's nine transits on 25 Sep, so resilience still depends on US escort and on which count is believed. Iran's strait authority threatening charterers on 26 Sep shows coercion moving to the commercial chain.

On deterrence versus proxy and deniable escalation, the Rising · Contested status is confirmed: Trump's 27 Sep expectation of talks this week against Tehran's 'no plan' reply keeps the Qatari channel as message-passing under an ultimatum, so layered pressure and unattributed claims substitute for direct escalation, keeping adaptability High.

27 Sep: At the second-anniversary ceremony for Nasrallah and Safieddine in Beirut's southern suburbs, attended by tens of thousands, Qassem said resistance will continue until the 'complete expulsion' of Israeli forces, that some 90,000 Israeli troops had failed to 'break the resistance', that 'we are ready for dialogue and discussion, but first, liberate the south', that 'direct negotiations with the enemy will bring nothing but defeat', and urged the state to end 'concessions' and suspend direct negotiations while acknowledging the president's legal authority over talks (Times of Israel; PressTV; Arab News).

Western diplomats told Asharq Al-Awsat that Washington blocked Lebanon's six-month UNIFIL extension request and wants the Lebanese army alone on the border (Asharq Al-Awsat, single source); UNIFIL logged 195 Israeli airspace violations between 22 and 25 Sep (Naharnet).

25 Sep: Salam told the UNGA that Israel must withdraw 'from all Lebanese territory' and that weapons must be 'held by the state alone' (Al Jazeera; Naharnet); an Israeli force raided the Sadana area outside Kfar Shuba and surrounded a farm, drones and artillery hit Kfartebnit, Nabatieh al-Fawqa, Wadi al-Hujeir and Majdal Zoun (Anadolu), a mass detonation was carried out at Deir Seryan and the IDF fired an interceptor at a 'false identification' (Naharnet; Times of Israel); Hezbollah's Fadlallah said the group is open to indirect talks but 'not through surrender' (Naharnet).

timeline.text: The United States, Israel and Lebanon signed a US-brokered Trilateral Framework tying phased Israeli withdrawal to Hezbollah disarmament and creating a trilateral military coordination group.
Lebanese army troops deployed in Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, the first of three US-supervised pilot zones, after Israeli forces pulled back from the village.
Israel detonated about 1,100 tonnes of explosives to destroy Hezbollah tunnels under Ali al-Taher ridge and declared its south Lebanon security zone complete.

Israeli tanks and stun grenades forced Lebanese soldiers off a new post outside Deir Mimas that Israel said lay inside its Yellow Line, and the dispute was referred to the Military Technical Committee.

A mass Israeli detonation at Khiam blacked out the Hasbaya, Shebaa and Arqoub areas and damaged homes and a school in Marjayoun, as Hezbollah's Mohammad Raad said the group fought on at Ali al-Taher to foil the framework's implementation mechanism.

Salam told the UN General Assembly that Israel must withdraw to the recognised borders and that weapons must be held by the state alone, a day after asking for a Security Council-mandated presence to avoid a vacuum after UNIFIL, while Israeli strikes, shelling and a mass detonation at Deir Seryan continued and the IDF fired an interceptor at what it later called a false identification.

The IDF struck a Hezbollah weapons store at Sejoud to remove what it called a threat to its troops in the security zone, artillery and reported phosphorus shelling continued across Tyre, Bint Jbeil and Nabatieh districts, and Western diplomats said Washington had blocked a six-month UNIFIL extension and wants the Lebanese army to hold the border alone.

Hezbollah launched an explosive drone at Israeli troops inside the security zone overnight without causing casualties, the Israeli air force struck drone and anti-tank launch sites across nine southern localities in response, and Qassem told a Nasrallah-anniversary crowd that resistance continues until full expulsion and that Israel must first liberate the south before any dialogue.

text: On border-zone security versus rocket, drone and dispersed-launch threats, the Established and Contested reading is borne out from Hezbollah's side for the first time since the 19 Sep roadside bomb: the explosive drone launched at troops inside the zone overnight on 26–27 Sep caused no casualties but drew Israeli strikes on nine localities from Nabatieh al-Fawqa to Beit Yahoun, and the IDF said it hit drone and anti-tank launch sites, so the dispersed-launch threat stays inside the zone. Qassem's 27 Sep line, 'first liberate the south', ties disarmament to withdrawal and signals continued harassment. On precision strike versus escalation control, the pattern is unchanged: the 27 Sep response was framed as removing launch sites under a 'committed to the agreement' line, yet it followed mass detonations at Khiam, Bint Jbeil and Deir Seryan on 23–25 Sep and phosphorus reports on 23 and 26 Sep, so restraint at the edge remains contradicted.

On ceasefire monitoring versus armed-group reconstitution, the trigger is closer to firing from the monitoring side: Lacroix said on 23 Sep the Council must decide 'rather soon than late' and diplomats said Washington opposes a UN-flagged successor, Asharq Al-Awsat reported on 26 Sep that a six-month extension was blocked (single source), and Qassem on 27 Sep urged the government to suspend direct negotiations, the track on which the framework's verification rests; adaptability stays Medium.

items.whyNow: Cambodia's podium reply to Anutin came on 26 Sep New York time (reported 27 Sep) when Prak Sokhonn told the UNGA that the conflict had 'seriously eroded trust', that more than 20,000 Cambodians still cannot go home, that Thailand should implement the Kuala Lumpur Declaration, the Fuxian Consensus and the 27 Dec joint statement and resume JBC demarcation, that Thailand's termination of the 2001 maritime MoU forced the UNCLOS conciliation, and that the Charter 'does not prescribe one standard for the powerful and another for the less powerful'; Khmer Times reports a Thai right of reply accusing Cambodia of 'unprovoked and indiscriminate' attacks (single source). Nothing moved on the line in the window, so the contest sits in forums and procurement plans ahead of the October Hague conciliation round, with the border fortified, walled and closed.
changes: 27 Sep (26 Sep New York): Prak Sokhonn delivered Cambodia's UNGA81 statement, saying recent tensions had 'seriously eroded trust and confidence', that over 20,000 Cambodian civilians cannot return home because of what Phnom Penh calls occupation and obstruction, calling for full implementation of the Kuala Lumpur Joint Declaration, the Fuxian Consensus and the 27 Dec 2025 joint statement and the 'prompt resumption' of JBC survey and demarcation, saying Cambodia was 'compelled' into UNCLOS conciliation after Thailand terminated the 2001 MoU in May, and stressing that the Charter 'does not prescribe one standard for the powerful and another for the less powerful' (AKP; Anadolu; Tempo; Phnom Penh Post; Khmer Times). Khmer Times reported that the two delegations 'traded blame' and that Thailand used a right of reply accusing Cambodia of 'unprovoked and indiscriminate armed attacks' in 2025 (Khmer Times, single source; no Thai outlet or the Thai UN mission had reported a UNGA81 reply by run time). A Phnom Penh Post opinion piece by Tesh Chanthorn, syndicated by The Star, argued that Anutin's call for peace needs 'respect for sovereignty, international law, existing agreements, credible evidence and the equal rights of all nations' (The Star / Phnom Penh Post).

24–25 Sep: PM Anutin told the UNGA on 24 Sep that Thailand 'has never sought conflict' and 'is engaging in good faith', that he and Hun Manet had agreed in May to settle border issues bilaterally but Cambodia instead launched compulsory UNCLOS conciliation, which concerns maritime delimitation only, and urged Phnom Penh to cooperate on border security, demining and online-scam networks (Thai PBS World; Nation Thailand; Bangkok Post; Khmer Times). The Aviationist published mission markings on 19 RTAF F-16s recording Mk.82, Mk.84, GBU-12 and KGGB employment in the July and December 2025 operations (The Aviationist, 25 Sep, single source).

23–24 Sep: Hun Manet told an international anti-scam conference in Phnom Penh on 23 Sep that scam crackdowns 'should not be used as a tool to attack other countries or as a pretext for military force' (Nation Thailand); Thailand's JIC chief ACM Prapas Sornchaidee replied on 24 Sep by urging implementation of Clause 10 (anti-scam cooperation) of the 27 Dec 2025 agreement, while Sihasak said the October Hague round 'will move on to the substance' and Prak Sokhonn called conciliation 'a means to rebuild trust, not a form of escalation' (Nation Thailand; Thai PBS World; Khmer Times).

22 Sep: Defence Security Asia reported that the RTAF's FY2026 procurement plan lists 20 Israeli Rampage air-launched rockets, 100 MPR-500 bombs and 50 Lizard III laser-guidance kits for its F-16s, about US$33m, framed as a stand-off answer to Cambodia's PHL-03 launchers; planned procurements, not confirmed contracts (Defence Security Asia, single source). Cambodia lodged a formal protest the same day over a Buddha statue placed by Thai troops and monks on 18 Sep at Phnom Beng, Anlong Veng, calling it another 'fait accompli' on occupied land (The Star / Phnom Penh Post).

21 Sep: In his International Day of Peace message Hun Manet urged Thailand to honour the agreements reached between the two countries and settle the border peacefully under international law, contrasting stalled talks with Thailand against 86% and 84% demarcation completed with Laos and Vietnam (Phnom Penh Post; Khmer Times).

21–27 Sep: No exchange of fire, drone crossing, incursion or mine casualty was reported in the window; the last military-technical items remain Cambodia's 15 Sep protest of a Thai trench near Boundary Pillar 9 and the 17 Sep Hill 450 trench settlement by liaison (Khmer Times; Khaosod English).

timeline.text: Thailand and Cambodia signed a ceasefire taking effect at noon, ending 20 days of fighting that killed over 100 people and displaced more than half a million.
Thailand's armed forces chief announced completion of the first 1.3 km of a permanent concrete border wall in Chanthaburi's Pong Nam Ron district, with over 7 km more planned.
Cambodia and Thailand delivered opening statements in Singapore before a UNCLOS Annex V conciliation commission on their overlapping claims in the Gulf of Thailand.

The first Singapore conciliation session closed with Cambodia tabling three settlement options and Thailand insisting a maritime boundary be delimited before any resource sharing; a second meeting was set for The Hague in October.
Cambodia formally protested a Buddha statue that Thai troops and monks placed on 18 September at Phnom Beng in Anlong Veng, calling it a fait accompli on occupied land.

Hun Manet told an international anti-scam conference in Phnom Penh that scam crackdowns must not become a pretext for military force against a neighbour; Thailand replied the next day by demanding implementation of the anti-scam clause of the December agreement.

Anutin told the UN General Assembly that Thailand regretted Cambodia's turn to UNCLOS conciliation after the two leaders had agreed in May to settle border issues bilaterally, and urged joint work on border security, demining and scam networks.

Prak Sokhonn told the UN General Assembly that the conflict had seriously eroded trust, that over 20,000 Cambodians still cannot return home, that Thailand should implement the December agreements and resume Joint Boundary Commission demarcation, and that the Charter sets no separate standard for powerful states.

text: On border incident management versus escalation prevention, the Declining / cautiously improving reading still holds: no exchange of fire, drone crossing or mine casualty was reported between 12 and 27 Sep, and friction is limited to the Boundary Pillar 9 trench protested on 15 Sep and the Phnom Beng statue protested on 22 Sep. The capability signal remains the 22 Sep report of Rampage rockets and precision kits in the RTAF's FY2026 plan (single source), which shows Thailand institutionalising stand-off strike against long-range rockets rather than changing behaviour on the line. On ceasefire monitoring versus local force autonomy, the trigger has not fired, but Prak Sokhonn's 26 Sep statement that more than 20,000 Cambodians still cannot return because of what Phnom Penh calls occupation and obstruction shows that consolidation of positions under the ceasefire, not fire, is now the central grievance.

On regional mediation versus bilateral military signalling, the Background monitor status is contradicted in one respect: the contest has moved to the UN podium, where Anutin on 24 Sep argued for bilateral mechanisms and Sokhonn on 26 Sep answered with the JBC, the December agreements and 'sovereign equality', while Khmer Times reports a Thai right of reply (single source). Neither side has convened the GBC or JBC this year, so the mechanisms both cite remain idle and ASEAN's observers are the only functioning channel; adaptability stays Low.

changes: 27 Sep: Human-rights group Justicia, Encuentro y Perdón said 39 political prisoners were freed between Friday 25 and Saturday 26 Sep from several prisons, among them eight women accused of 'narco-terrorism' in 2021, six people accused of working with the US in the 2020 'Operation Gideon' attempt and student Wilder Vásquez, jailed since 2018; Clippve counted seven releases on Saturday morning; the releases followed a government–opposition negotiating session on Friday held with US approval, the government made no statement, Rubio has put releases since January at over 1,000, Foro Penal still listed 344 political prisoners on 18 Sep and JEP says about 450 remain (Al Jazeera/AFP; AP via ABC News; BBC via aggregators).

27 Sep: Comando con Venezuela's 'gran caravana' brought hundreds of people on motorcycles, in cars and on foot into the streets of Zulia (Maracaibo), Falcón, Lara, Barinas, Apure, Mérida, Bolívar, Guárico, Carabobo, Miranda (Los Teques) and La Guaira to demand Machado's safe return, an electoral calendar and a 2027 presidential vote; National Guard officers intercepted Vente Venezuela organiser Fernando Torrealba during the Maracaibo caravan and his whereabouts were unknown afterwards; Juan Pablo Guanipa said the movement would channel discontent into 'a democratic electoral process' and Machado said from Panama 'I will return very soon to my country' (Infobae; El Diario; Efecto Cocuyo).

26 Sep: Rodríguez marked the 21st anniversary of the armed forces' Strategic Operational Command (Ceofanb) with a message praising troops 'deployed firmly to guarantee the general welfare and political stability' and stressing 'cohesion between the national executive and the military institution', with no reference to the United States or elections (teleSUR; El Universal). Reuters reported she returned from the UN week with 'no concrete agreements' and no election date, that Rubio said the project must 'culminate in a free and fair election', that experts put a credible vote at least 12 months away and that the IDB's $2.5bn bridge loan still faces board opposition (Reuters via US News); Trump said at the White House 'I spoke about elections' with her (Reuters via Internazionale). A Guardian investigation relayed by Portside argued the NABEP deal is 'likely doomed' on legal, logistical and authority grounds, Venezuelan law capping contracts at 25 years and the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital lacking authority to hold equity (Portside, single source).

26 Sep: Chief government negotiator Jorge Rodríguez denied that the authorities are blocking Machado's return and said parliamentary, municipal, gubernatorial and presidential elections would be held within the constitutional timeframe (El Nacional); Machado's platform called the 27 Sep caravan after her flight from Panama 'never even took off' because Bonaire, Aruba and Curaçao refused landing permission (EFE via Infobae). A Wall Street Journal report relayed by Rio Times says the Pentagon-backed NABEP produces about 220,000 b/d against Chevron's 280,000 and plans to add 180,000 b/d next year (Rio Times, single source). No JTF-WHEM strike has been reported since the 70th on 19 Sep (Just Security timeline, updated 20 Sep).

21–23 Sep: Rodríguez told the UNGA on 23 Sep 'there will be elections' in an 'orderly, institutional and verifiable' transition and thanked Trump for restoring cooperation (UN News); Chile's Kast agreed to restore ties step by step (El Nacional); Reuters reported on 22 Sep that IDB president Goldfajn is working on a $2.5bn Special Development Lending loan requiring size and IMF-programme waivers and facing board pushback (Reuters via Investing.com).

history.note: Baseline: post-January 2026 operation; transition under US pressure.

timeline.text: US forces captured President Nicolás Maduro and his wife in overnight strikes across Caracas and three other states, flying them to New York to face narco-terrorism charges.
US-backed talks between Delcy Rodríguez's interim government and an opposition delegation led by Dinorah Figuera opened in Caracas, with Jorge Rodríguez heading the government side.
The White House announced 100-year concessions on 17 Venezuelan oil fields to North American Blue Energy Partners, with the US government taking a 35 percent stake.
Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere struck a go-fast vessel on Caribbean narco-trafficking routes, killing four, in the 70th US counter-cartel maritime strike.

Trump held a pull-aside meeting with interim President Delcy Rodríguez at a UN General Assembly reception, their first encounter since Maduro's capture, covering debt restructuring; the same day Machado's team said three attempts to leave Panama for Venezuela had failed within 24 hours, her seventh blocked return.

Addressing the UN General Assembly, Rodríguez pledged elections and a transition to 'full democracy' and said dialogue with the opposition had opened, but gave no date; Chile's Kast met her the same week to begin restoring consular ties.

Rodríguez returned from New York with no concrete deals and no election date as Trump said he had raised elections with her, the government's negotiator denied blocking Machado, and Machado's movement called a nationwide caravan for 27 September after Bonaire, Aruba and Curaçao refused her flight landing rights.

Rights groups reported 39 political prisoners freed on 25–26 September after a government–opposition negotiating session, and opposition caravans in about eleven states demanded Machado's return and a 2027 election while the National Guard detained a Vente Venezuela organiser in Maracaibo.

text: On counter-criminal operations versus sovereignty and escalation, the trigger has not fired: no JTF-WHEM strike has been reported since the 70th on 19 Sep, and Rodríguez's 26 Sep message to the Strategic Operational Command stressed 'cohesion' between the executive and the military without mentioning the United States, a consolidation signal rather than confrontation. On border and maritime control versus illicit networks, the Established status is borne out at a lower rate, with two Caribbean strikes and two Pacific refuelling-vessel interdictions in September and an eight-day pause since.

infoOps.question: Is Beijing, or Washington, using information operations or strategic communications to pressure Taiwan in the wake of the Trump–Xi summit; through which channels; and how is Taipei responding?

feed.query: (Taiwan OR Taipei) ("cognitive warfare" OR disinformation OR "information operations" OR "information warfare" OR propaganda OR "united front" OR "Taiwan Affairs Office" OR "state media" OR "Global Times" OR Xinhua OR "influence operation" OR "fact check" OR narrative OR "psychological warfare" OR "strategic communication" OR "oppose Taiwan independence")

findings.actor: Taiwan national security official (via Taipei Times)
findings.text: On 28 Sep 2026 a Taiwanese national security official briefed that Beijing 'failed to gain traction' in pressing Washington to reduce arms sales and secured no tariff or high-tech relief, and that China had hoped to frame US-China ties as a stable relationship 'between equal powers' to deflect from economic problems. The official predicted that, lacking substantive wins, Beijing 'might turn to propaganda, using images of Xi receiving the red-carpet welcome to promote narratives that China is rising', and urged Taiwan to strengthen its 'silicon shield' and asymmetric defence (single source).

findings.actor: Taiwan Mainland Affairs Council (deputy minister Shen Yu-chung)
findings.text: On 27-28 Sep 2026 the MAC's Shen Yu-chung said Beijing had tried to place Taiwan inside US-China 'constructive strategic stability' but that Xi's push for a breakthrough on the strait 'did not go smoothly', and that Xi may have sought to trade cooperation on Iran for concessions on Taiwan, which Trump did not accept. He cited Ambassador Perdue's statement that Taiwan and Iran 'should be handled separately' as carrying 'subtext', turning the US envoy's words into Taipei's rebuttal of Beijing's linkage narrative.

findings.actor: KMT (legislator Lee Yen-hsiu) and DPP government (Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung)
findings.text: On 28 Sep 2026 KMT legislator Lee Yen-hsiu said the summit had made the 'anti-China card' that Washington and Taipei could jointly play 'ineffective', describing a 'G2' framework in which Trump deals transactionally under 'America First', and urged the DPP to seek concrete gains on chip tariffs, arms-sale approvals and diplomatic space instead. Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung replied that Taiwan and the US should manage China together rather than accept 'US-China joint management of Taiwan', keeping the opposition's 'G2' reading and the government's 'true partner' line in contest before the November elections.

On 27 Sep 2026 Wu said 'it would be in the US' vital interests to move the arms sales forward', that supporting Taiwan's democracy and self-defence aligns with 'mainstream countries', and that 'China has been aggressively pursuing narrative diplomacy' which the ministry will counter, citing the 21 Sep US-Japan-ROK and 22 Sep eight-nation statements on the strait. The ministry thus named Beijing's post-summit framing as a narrative campaign and set allied statements against it.

On 27 Sep 2026 Senator Ricketts, chair of the Senate Foreign Relations East Asia subcommittee, backed the US$14 billion US-Taiwan arms package on Fox's 'Sunday Briefing' as a means to deter China, alongside remarks on possible sanctions on Chinese banks over Iran. On 16 Sep he had said the US 'will not tolerate' a change in Taiwan's status by force and that clearing the roughly US$30 billion delivery backlog is the first priority; the Fox appearance keeps congressional pressure on the White House in public view (single source).

findings.actor: PLA (per ROC Ministry of National Defense)
findings.text: In the 24 hours to 06:00 on 27 Sep 2026 Taiwan's MND reported 2 PLA aircraft sorties, 5 PLAN ships and 6 official ships, after 5 sorties, 6 PLAN ships, 5 official ships and one median-line crossing in the northern ADIZ the day before; September stood at 215 aircraft and 269 ship sightings by 26 Sep. Air pressure has stayed at or below five sorties a day since the summit while ships hold at ten to eleven, a restrained posture that leaves Beijing's message to the diplomatic channel.

On 26 Sep 2026 Trump told reporters before leaving the White House that he and Xi 'didn't talk about it too much. Right now, it's fine. It's just moving along', adding 'he understands very much how I feel'. He neither restated the US 'does not support' formula nor accepted Xi's 'oppose independence' wording, leaving Beijing's readout as the fuller public account of the exchange.

findings.actor: US Ambassador to China David Perdue
findings.text: After the summit Perdue said 'there's no change in the Taiwan policy here. We're not changing the language. We're not changing our position there', citing the one-China policy, Taiwan Relations Act, three communiques and Six Assurances (reported 27 Sep). A State Department spokesperson had said on 25 Sep that policy is unchanged and the US will 'stand with' Indo-Pacific partners 'which includes Taiwan'.

On 26 Sep 2026 People's Daily's 'Zhong Sheng' commentary called Taiwan 'the core of China's core interests' and 'the first red line that cannot be crossed' in China-US relations, urged Washington to 'maintain the correct stance of opposing Taiwan independence', and cast 'constructive strategic stability' as a vision both leaders should 'transform into concrete action'. It kept Xi's summit wording in circulation after the White House fact sheet omitted Taiwan.

On 26 Sep 2026 the MAC rejected the White House fact sheet's line that the US and China 'were allies in World War II and fought side by side', saying the PRC 'did not even exist' before 1949, that the ROC was the true ally and that the CCP devoted 'one part' of its effort to fighting Japan. It also refused to let Taiwan be folded into US-China 'strategic stability' and cited PLA harassment east of Taiwan as the real threat to the status quo.

A Global Times English editorial on 25 Sep 2026, closing out coverage of Xi's state visit, called Taiwan 'the most important and sensitive core issue in China-US relations' and repeated Xi's hope that the US will 'uphold the correct stance of opposing Taiwan independence'. It aimed Beijing's summit line at foreign readers.

According to the PRC MFA readout of the 24 Sep 2026 White House talks, Xi told Trump that China's position on reunification is 'clear-cut' and that the US should 'adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence' and 'handle the Taiwan question with caution'. This goes beyond the long-standing US 'do not support' wording. On 25 Sep, Taiwan's MOFA rejected it as 'distorting facts and unilaterally conveying its own positions'.

assessment.text: Evidence for 24 to 28 Sep 2026 shows Beijing pressing Taiwan through the summit record rather than documented covert activity, and Taipei now contesting that record. Xi's 'oppose Taiwan independence' request (PRC MFA, 24 Sep) was carried by Global Times on 25 Sep and People's Daily on 26 Sep, while the PLA held air activity to two to five sorties a day; no state-media line dated 27-28 Sep and no fact-check or NSB count of inauthentic activity was found. Washington stayed ambiguous, Trump saying on 26 Sep only that Xi 'understands very much how I feel' and Perdue that the language is unchanged. Taipei shifted from rebuttal to claiming the outcome: on 27 Sep MOFA named Beijing's 'narrative diplomacy' as something to counter, and on 28 Sep the MAC said Xi's 'strategic stability' and Iran-for-Taiwan framings 'did not go smoothly' and a security official predicted red-carpet 'China is rising' propaganda. The KMT's 28 Sep 'G2' reading shows the domestic channel still open to Beijing's framing.

changes: 27 Sep: former foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya left Haneda for Beijing at the head of a 50-member delegation of the Japan Association for the Promotion of International Trade for a 27-30 Sep visit meant to 'help break the deadlock' in ties; meetings with senior Chinese officials, and a hoped-for audience with Xi, were still being arranged and no Chinese comment had been published by early 28 Sep (Nikkei Asia; Jiji/nippon.com).

26-27 Sep: Sankei reported satellite analysis by the Kokkiken (JINF) think-tank showing the PLA has built mock targets resembling the ASDF's E-767 AWACS, F-35 and F-2 at a range north of Lop Nur, Xinjiang: construction seen from July 2025, a mock apron finished in November and the targets erected in January 2026; researcher Nakagawa Maki said targets aimed only at the JSDF had been absent since 2023 and that the timing after Takaichi took office suggests a signal meant to be seen on satellite imagery as well as training; a 22 Sep US open-source analysis had separately identified E-767, F-35, F-16 and Patriot mock-ups in the Xinjiang desert (Sankei via headtopics; Asiae; Herald Economy; Brady Africk).

27 Sep: four gun-armed China Coast Guard ships (1301, 1303, 1304, 1307) sailed in the Senkaku contiguous zone for the 50th consecutive day, 30-36 km off Taisho and Kuba islands at 9 am, warned off by Japan Coast Guard patrol vessels; no territorial-water entry (Naigai Times, single source).

27 Sep: a Maritime Executive editorial reported that PLA Daily ran four stories attacking Japan's defence expansion during Xi's Washington visit against one on the summit, casting Japan as an 'enemy country' under the UN Charter, and that Defence Minister Koizumi has said infrastructure for a permanent Chu-SAM (Type-03) air-defence presence on Yonaguni will be in place by 2030 alongside Mogami-class frigate and submarine expansion (Maritime Executive, single source on the PLA Daily count).

26 Sep: Trump called Takaichi for about 20 minutes to debrief her on the Xi meeting and the two confirmed Japan-US cooperation on China 'including economic security and defence', Takaichi calling the two countries 'the most trustworthy allies' after the White House fact sheet described the US and China as 'allies in World War II' (Jiji/nippon.com; Sankei; Japan Times).

21-24 Sep: Guo Jiakun called the US Typhon deployment in Kyushu 'accelerated remilitarization' and defended the UN 'enemy state' clauses against Takaichi's 22 Sep UN speech; China's defence ministry told Japan to stop 'sowing discord' in the South China Sea as JS Ise sailed in the ADMM-Plus formation; a Japan Times-obtained document showed US and Japanese officials met on 10 Sep on the yttrium squeeze, which the summit left unresolved (PRC MFA; Xinhua; China Military; Japan Times; Digitimes).

At the White House Trump called the US and China 'allies during World War II' and Xi said they had 'stood shoulder to shoulder' against fascist aggression, as Beijing's foreign and defence ministries rejected Takaichi's 'enemy state' call and accused Japan of remilitarisation.

Trump debriefed Takaichi on the Xi meeting in a 20-minute call and the two confirmed cooperation on China including economic security and defence, while Sankei reported think-tank satellite analysis showing PLA mock targets of the E-767, F-35 and F-2 at a range north of Lop Nur since January.

text: On maritime and air encounters versus escalation management, the Established · Contested watch area shows presence without incident: four gun-armed coast guard ships sailed the Senkaku contiguous zone on 27 Sep for a 50th consecutive day and were warned off without a territorial-water entry (single source); incident management stayed untested. On alliance interoperability versus contested access, the Rising status is reinforced from both sides: the 26 Sep Trump-Takaichi call confirmed cooperation 'including economic security and defence', Koizumi's plan for permanent Chu-SAM infrastructure on Yonaguni by 2030 was singled out by PLA Daily during Xi's visit (single source), and Sankei reported on 26-27 Sep that mock-ups of the E-767, F-35 and F-2 have stood at a range north of Lop Nur since January. Access is secured by reassurance and island fortification that Beijing now rehearses against.

On information and legal narratives versus coercive faits accomplis, the Established rating is confirmed: the desert mock-ups were read by the Kokkiken analysts as a signal to the Takaichi government as much as training, PLA Daily ran four attacks on Japan's build-up for one story on the summit, and the yttrium squeeze stands. Iwaya's delegation, in Beijing from 27 Sep, is the only thaw channel; adaptability stays Medium because Japan answers with coalitions and back channels while China holds narrative, minerals and the target range.

items.whyNow: On 27 Sep Defence Minister Rajnath Singh told the NDTV Defence Conclave that 'as long as our neighbour continues the state policy of terrorism, India is completely ready for every kind of strike against terrorism' and Modi used Mann Ki Baat to tie the 2016 surgical strikes, Balakot and Operation Sindoor into one counter-terror line ahead of the 28 Sep tenth anniversary, while ISPR claimed 71-plus 'India-backed' militants killed in Balochistan over 96 hours; the exchange is still verbal, the Line of Control is quiet and Tarang Shakti's operational phase opened at Jodhpur with US F-35s.
changes: 27 Sep: Rajnath Singh told the NDTV Defence Conclave that 'as long as our neighbour continues the state policy of terrorism, India is completely ready for every kind of strike against terrorism', that 'the scope of dialogue ends' where a country shelters terrorism against India, and that India 'will not compromise on its security under any circumstances'; in Mann Ki Baat Modi said the 2016 surgical strikes 'demonstrated a new example of India's counter-terrorism policy' and that 'from the Balakot airstrike to Operation Sindoor' terror will draw 'a befitting response', ahead of the 28 Sep tenth anniversary (ANI/Daily Excelsior; The Tribune; Kashmir Observer).

27 Sep: ISPR said 'more than 71 terrorists' of 'Fitna al-Khawarij' and 'Fitna al-Hindustan' were killed in 96 hours of Operation Shaban and related actions in Quetta's Shaban area, Ziarat, Nushki and Mand, calling them 'India-backed' and alleging Afghan Taliban involvement 'backed and sponsored by India'; no independent verification of the toll or the attribution (Geo News; KabulNow; TRT World).

27 Sep: The IAF opened the operational phase of Tarang Shakti at Jodhpur (to 12 Oct) with Australia, the US, the UAE, France, Germany, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh flying F-35s, Rafales, F-16s, A400M, MRTT and C-130s near the Pakistan border; the F-35 count still conflicts between two-three (Tribune/ANI) and six (UNI) (DD News; UNI; The Tribune).

26 Sep: Jaishankar told the UNGA that 'a serial practitioner of terrorism misrepresented facts before this assembly' and that India's 'right to defend ourselves against terrorism will be exercised'; India's right of reply (Petal Gahlot) warned 'terror will have consequences' and Pakistan's counter-reply (Saima Saleem) accused India of 'weaponising water' and exporting terrorism; Defence Security Asia separately reported Pakistan receiving the 2,000 km Baykar K2 kamikaze UAV (single source, no official confirmation) (The Tribune; Dawn; Defence Security Asia).

26 Sep: Pakistan Navy ships HUNAIN and YARMOOK seized more than 2,800 kg of narcotics worth about $750 million from a boat in the Arabian Sea, with Zardari, Sharif and Naqvi praising the Navy; PNS Hunain is the vessel that collided with INS Kolkata on 15 Sep, so the ship is back on operational patrol with no further India–Pakistan naval incident reported (The Express Tribune; Pakistan Today).

25 Sep: Sharif told the UNGA that any attempt to 'stop, impede or divert' Pakistan's Indus share 'will be treated as an act of war' and called Kashmir Pakistan's 'jugular vein'; the same day Army chief Gen Dhiraj Seth reviewed Chinar Corps formations along the Line of Control and hinterland counter-terrorist preparedness, commending troops for 'a high state of vigilance' with no infiltration figures released (Dawn; UN News; ANI; The Week).

timeline.text: A Hague Court of Arbitration unanimously rules the Indus Waters Treaty remains fully in force and bars India from raising the Ratle dam; India rejects the award within hours as 'illegally constituted'.
Pakistani troops fire small arms and mortars across the Line of Control in Poonch's Mankote sector, a day after firing in Krishna Ghati; the Indian Army retaliates.

Indian destroyer INS Kolkata and Pakistani patrol vessel PNS Hunain collide in the North Arabian Sea during Pakistan's SEASPARK-26 exercise, the first physical military incident since May 2025; each side summons the other's charge d'affaires the next day and India later rejects Pakistan's account as 'the usual prevarication'.
Two Pakistani Jaish-e-Mohammad militants are killed overnight in 'Operation Sohan' in the Majalta forests of Udhampur, Jammu, and a suspected over-ground worker is detained.

India's envoy at the UN Human Rights Council tells Pakistan that 'neither terror nor theatrics' will repay its loans, New Delhi restates that the Indus arbitration court is illegally constituted, and Dar tells the OIC Contact Group that the treaty is binding under the August award.

timeline.text: Min Aung Hlaing is inaugurated as president of Myanmar's quasi-civilian military government in Naypyitaw, and on 21 April offers armed groups peace talks with a 100-day deadline that the KNU, CNF and NUG reject.
The military launches 'Operation 4926', a combined land, naval and air offensive against the Arakan Army across Sittwe, Ponnagyun, Kyaukphyu and Gwa townships in Rakhine State.
Six fibre-optic FPV drones strike Tada-U airbase near Mandalay; resistance says Yak-130 jets were hit, the junta says all were intercepted, and international flights are cancelled.
The Arakan Army's counter-offensive seizes four junta outposts on the Sittwe-Ponnagyun border, including positions near Minchaung Bridge and the Shwe Min Gan naval station.

A junta column of over 180 vehicles and about 1,000 troops with MLRS, drones and signal jammers reaches the DDI 25 weapons plant in Saw Township to renew the offensive on Mindat and Kanpetlet in southern Chin State.

Three junta jets bomb the National Unity Government's regional command near Kyaikto, killing at least six including Air Force defector Nay Win Aung, as the Arakan Army repels a two-week junta attempt on the Maei pass at Mindon, Malaysia sets 29 Sep to begin deporting Myanmar migrants, Myanmar recalls its ambassador to Thailand, a Delhi court lets the foreign drone trainers leave India and an MNDAA delegation opens Chinese-pressed talks in Naypyidaw.

Ground fighting resumes on the Sittwe–Ponnagyun border after a four-day pause forced by junta losses on 21 Sep, with jets and Y-12s bombing Yae Yo Pyin, War Bo and Pauktaw, while residents on the Rakhine–Ayeyarwady border report the junta trucking hundreds of casualties nightly from Thabaung to Pathein.

Bangladesh's Coast Guard seizes 22 tonnes of Myanmar-origin iron and battery scrap at Patenga and detains seven men, days after intercepting Rakhine-bound urea, as a fact-check rejects claims that the MNDAA–junta talks in Naypyidaw have collapsed.

text: On distributed resistance versus state airpower, the Established · Contested status holds: stalled pushes restart under air cover without gaining ground. On 26 Sep fighting resumed on the Sittwe–Ponnagyun border after a four-day pause forced by the 21 Sep losses, with jets and Y-12s bombing Yae Yo Pyin, War Bo and Pauktaw (single source), while the same day's strikes on Gwa, Hpruso, Mindat and Kanpetlet hit houses and monasteries without the DDI 25 column moving. The Deputy Defence Minister told parliament on 25 Sep that artists, professionals, businesspeople and their children will be conscripted, and Mon State's 28th intake press-ganged 222 men. On commercial UAS and improvised systems versus conventional advantage, the Rising status is borne out on the regime side: a 26 Sep drone-bomb on a Kanbalu monastery and the 24 Sep Kyaikto strike that killed an Air Force defector (coordinates the regime says came from informants) show cheap air systems and human targeting being institutionalised on both sides.

On fragmented governance versus logistics and civilian resilience, the Established status is reinforced by corridors: Beijing kept the MNDAA at the Naypyidaw table (a 27 Sep fact-check rejected claims the talks collapsed), Bangladesh seized 22 tonnes of Myanmar scrap at Patenga on 27 Sep, and Malaysia's 29 Sep deportation flight tests ASEAN's line. changes: 27 Sep: Schools in Riyadh moved to remote learning on the Madrasati platform from Sunday to Thursday, with at least three schools messaging parents on Saturday and the Ministry of Education giving no public reason, a day after the interceptions over the capital and Khamis Mushait; the Houthis have launched at Saudi cities on 19, 24 and 26 Sep (The National, The Media Line, AFP via CP24).

27 Sep: Yemen armed forces spokesman Col. Majid al-Nuzaili said 756 operations over 72 hours across the Kataf, Al-Baqa, Alab, Al-Jawf, Marib, Al-Bayda, Lahj and Taiz fronts killed or wounded 2,316 Houthis and killed four Iranian experts in drone and missile launching in Taiz (party claims, unverified); Al Jazeera reported government forces taking Jabal Bazel, a height overlooking Houthi supply lines in southern Taiz, air raids on five Houthi positions and 146,000 displaced since July (Arab News, Al Arabiya, Al Jazeera).

26 Sep: From about 04:00 coalition spokesman al-Maliki announced the interception of two Houthi drones headed for Riyadh and two ballistic missiles aimed at Khamis Mushait, with alerts for Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Abha; Saree claimed 27 Saudi air strikes on bridges and roads across Taiz, Marib, Saada, Amran, Ibb and Hajjah including the al-Dalil bridge on the Sanaa–Taiz supply route, Saudi and Yemeni drones struck weapons depots in Marib, and Houthi officials threatened Saudi command-and-control sites if 'red lines' were crossed (Arab News, The National, Critical Threats).

26 Sep: GCC secretary general Al Budaiwi called the attacks a 'grave escalation'; Saudi FM Faisal bin Farhan told the UNGA the kingdom rejects the use of Hormuz, the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab 'as an instrument of pressure' and welcomed a 25 Sep Security Council condemnation of the Houthi attacks; Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera Houthi actions are 'not connected to Iran' and offered mediation; Iraq reached an understanding with Washington to continue dollar shipments (Asharq Al-Awsat, Arab News, Al Jazeera, Times of Israel live).

25 Sep: Yemen's President al-Alimi called for general mobilisation and offered Houthi defectors amnesty from 26 Sep; the Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani chiefs of staff met in Riyadh under the Makkah pact and agreed to integrate defensive capabilities; Iraq's PM al-Zaidi told the UNGA that weapons 'must remain in the hands of constitutional institutions' and that the coalition's end shifts relations 'from military cooperation to economic and development cooperation' (France 24, Arab News, Asharq Al-Awsat).

Ahead of the 30 September coalition exit from Iraq, the prime minister moves militia disarmament to a phased plan ending in June 2027 behind a 90-day halt in attacks, as Syrian President Sharaa says security talks with Israel reached about 90 percent before Israel pulled back.

After the Houthis fire a mixed missile and drone barrage at Jazan, Yanbu, Taif and Riyadh and Saudi Arabia intercepts six ballistic missiles, President Macron announces French soldiers, radars and air-defence systems for the Yanbu terminal and the Makkah pact foreign ministers agree in New York to convene their chiefs of staff.

The coalition intercepts two Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at the Khamis Mushait air base and two drones headed for Riyadh a day after Yemen's president declares general mobilisation and the Makkah-pact chiefs of staff meet in Riyadh, and the GCC calls the attacks a grave escalation.

Riyadh's schools switch to a week of remote learning after the interceptions, a strike on a market at Taiz's Mawiya junction kills at least seven by Houthi count, and Yemen's army claims 756 operations and four Iranian experts killed over 72 hours.

text: On long-range attack versus layered protection, the Rising · Contested status is borne out. Houthi salvos at Saudi cities on 19, 24 and 26 Sep were each fully intercepted by the coalition's account, yet on 27 Sep Riyadh's schools moved online for a week without an official reason, so the operational effect now runs through disruption, not damage. The counter remains institutional: the French Yanbu detachment announced on 24 Sep still had no dates and the Makkah-pact chiefs named no battery on 25 Sep, while Saudi air power on 26 Sep hit bridges on the Sanaa–Taiz supply route (Houthi claim of 27 strikes, single source) and a 27 Sep strike at Taiz's Mawiya market drew Saree's 'severe consequences' warning. On maritime disruption versus route resilience, the Established · Contested status holds: Bab al-Mandab stays Houthi-held, the government's claimed Jabal Bazel gain on 27 Sep and 756 operations in 72 hours (single source) target the highlands over the strait, and no new crossing count or ship attack was reported, so routings stay open under Saudi-specific pressure.

On regional basing versus militia targeting, the Established · Contested status tilts to host-nation management: al-Zaidi told the UN on 25 Sep that weapons must sit with constitutional institutions and the coalition's end moves relations to economic cooperation, days before the Erbil exit, with Israel–Syria unchanged since Sharaa's 90 percent remark.
